## Definition of Sthāyibhāva
An emotion that cannot be obscured by another opposing emotion and remains stable by its own nature is called "Sthāyibhāva" (Stable Emotion).

## Classification of Sthāyibhāva
Rati (Delight), Hāsa (Laughter), Soka (Sorrow), Kodha (Anger), Ussāha (Energy), Bhaya (Fear), Jigucchā (Disgust), Vimhaya (Wonder), and Sama (Tranquillity) are the nine types of Sthāyibhāva.

## Definition of Vyabhicāribhāva
Those emotions that occur habitually, moving towards the Sthāyibhāva through specific characteristics such as disappearance and appearance, are called "Vyabhicāribhāva" (Transitory Emotions).

## Classification of Vyabhicāribhāva
These are the thirty-three types: Nibbeda (Self-disparagement), Takka (Reasoning), Saṅkā (Doubt), Sama (Fatigue), Dhiti (Contentment), Jaḷatā (Stupidity), Dīnatā (Depression), Uggatta (Fierceness), Alasatta (Laziness), Sutta (Sleep), Tāsa (Terror), Gilāni (Debility), Ukka (Anxiety), Harisa (Joy), Sati (Recollection), Issā (Envy), Visāda (Despair), Avahitthā (Dissimulation), Cintā (Reflection), Gabba (Pride), Apamāra (Epilepsy/Madness), Amarisa (Impatience), Mada (Intoxication), Mati (Intellect), Ummāda (Insanity), Moha (Delusion), Vibodha (Awakening), Niddā (Slumber), Āvega (Agitation), Viḷā (Shame), Maraṇa (Death), Capala (Inconstancy), and Vyādhi (Sickness).

## Definition of Sāttvikabhāva
The state arising from a well-composed mind is called "Sattva." The emotions produced by this quality of Sattva are known as "Sāttvikabhāva" (Temperamental Emotions). Although these Sāttvikabhāvas exist as Anubhāva (consequents/effects), they are a distinct type of emotion separate from Sthāyibhāva and Vyabhicāribhāva.
